MultisolverFemur.content:
- **Authors:** Alisdair R MacLeod; Hannah Rose; Harinderjit S Gill.
- **Year:** 2016.
- **Journal:** *J Biomech Eng.* 2016 Dec 1;138(12).
- **DOI:** 10.1115/1.4034653.
- **Species:** Fourth-generation Sawbones® composite femurs; no animal species is specified.
- **Sample/model counts:** One generic FE model and four specimen-specific FE models created from CT scans. Experimental specimen count is not explicitly stated.
- **Loading/pressures:** Not specified.
- **Measurements:** Strain gauges at four locations; strain predictions compared with experimental results. Geometric variability in cortical thickness around the femoral neck was also evaluated.
- **Material assignment and values:** Not specified.
- **FE solvers:** Abaqus, ANSYS, and FEBio.
- **Boundary conditions:** Not specified.
- **Agreement and comparison results:** Strain predictions were within an average of **3.0%** across all three solvers (**r² > 0.99**) and **1.4%** for the two commercial codes. Average root mean squared error against experimental results was **134.5% (r² = 0.29)** for the generic model and **13.8% (r² = 0.96)** for specimen-specific models.
- **Main conclusions:** The three solvers showed excellent agreement. Specimen-specific models matched experimental results better than the generic model. Femoral-neck cortical thickness varied by up to **48.4%**. The study presented an experimentally validated femur FE model for all three solvers, freely available online with supporting validation data.
- **Limitations:** No explicit limitations are stated in the visible content.
- **Tongue-pressure findings:** Not applicable; this is not a tongue-pressure study.
- **Visible content:** Abstract only; full text is not shown.

FEBioAbaqusBiphasic.content:
- **Authors:** Qingen Meng, Zhongmin Jin, John Fisher, Ruth Wilcox.
- **Year / journal / DOI:** 2013; *Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers, Part H: Journal of Engineering in Medicine*, 227(9):1009–1019; **10.1177/0954411913483537**.
- **Species:** Not stated. **Sample size (n):** Not stated.
- **Full text:** Full text is visible.
- **Models and loading:** Porous flat-ended indentation: cartilage radius 15 mm, thickness 3.0 mm; indenter radius approximately 3 mm; displacement 0.15 or 0.54 mm (5% or 18% compression), applied over 2 s, then held 1200 s. Spherical-ended indentation: cartilage thickness 2 mm, bone thickness 5 mm, cartilage-pin radius 4.5 mm, indenter radius 1.5 mm; load 0.22 or 0.7 N (approximately 10% or 20% compression), ramped over 2 s, then held 1200 s. Joint contact: two 2-mm cartilage layers; curvature radii 25.5 and 26 mm; displacement 0.04 or 0.2 mm (1% or 5%), applied over 10 s, then held 300 s. Numerical pressure magnitudes are not provided.
- **Measurements:** Reaction force, fluid pressure, indenter displacement, and contact pressure.
- **Materials:** Cartilage Young’s modulus 0.54 MPa, Poisson’s ratio 0, void ratio 4.0 (solidity 0.2), permeability 0.004 mm⁴/N·s. Bone, when modeled: elastic modulus 2.0 GPa, Poisson’s ratio 0.2. Indenters rigid.
- **Solvers:** Abaqus 6.9-EF1 and FEBio 1.5.0.
- **Boundary conditions:** Cartilage base bonded/constrained; specified free-draining surfaces and no flow through bonded bone surfaces or symmetry planes. Contact-dependent surface fluid-flow conditions were used; Abaqus required user subroutines, whereas FEBio applied them automatically.
- **Comparison:** Mean differences, FEBio versus Abaqus: flat indentation reaction force 0.3%/1.0%, fluid pressure 0.7%/1.0%; spherical indentation displacement 1.1%/1.4%, pressure 2.5%/2.3%; joint pressure 2.0%/5.4%, contact pressure 7.0%/7.6%. Sensitivity cases: maximum mean differences 3.1% for pressure and 1.4% for displacement.
- **Conclusions / limitations:** Results agreed closely across tested models and material ranges; Abaqus without contact-flow subroutines produced different pressure distributions. Limitations: low fluid/contact pressures versus physiological expectations; only three relatively simple models, excluding collagen-fiber direction and nonlinear permeability. No tongue-pressure, tongue-stress/strain/displacement, or growth/remodeling findings are reported.

KneeTransferable.content:
- **Authors:** Alexander Paz; José J. García; Rami K. Korhonen; Mika E. Mononen.
- **Year / journal / DOI:** 2023; *Annals of Biomedical Engineering* (*Ann Biomed Eng*), 51, 2192–2203; 10.1007/s10439-023-03252-8.
- **Species:** Human.
- **Sample:** 78 Osteoarthritis Initiative participants; 154 knees. Models used healthy-baseline knees (Kellgren–Lawrence grade 0 or 1), classified by grade at 8-year follow-up.
- **Loading and measurements:** Simulated gait stance phase using generic effective axial joint force and knee-flexion trajectory. Axial force was scaled to body weight; the medial compartment was assumed to bear half the joint reaction force. No load or pressure magnitudes are reported. MRI-derived medial–lateral maximum condylar distance (M–L), medial-condyle anterior–posterior distance (A–P), and joint-space width (JS) were used to scale models; age and weight were also used.
- **Material and solvers:** ABAQUS Standard v.2018 used an experimentally validated fibril-reinforced poroviscoelastic (FRPVE) cartilage formulation. FEBio 3.3.2 used a fibril-reinforced biphasic formulation with properties selected to reproduce the ABAQUS material’s instantaneous response. Both used the same depth-dependent collagen-fibril orientation. Numerical material-property values are not provided in the page content.
- **Boundary conditions:** Ligaments, tendons, muscles, and meniscus were not explicitly modeled. Anterior–posterior and medial–lateral translations and internal–external rotations were fixed. Meniscus support force was subtracted from the joint force.
- **Cross-solver results:** Contact-area average maximum principal stress was essentially the same; ABAQUS stress peaks averaged 27% higher than FEBio. ABAQUS overstressed volumes were about 43% greater for corresponding KL groups; software differences were significant (*p* < 0.01). Both distinguished healthy from severe OA knees, AUC = 0.73. Runtime: 123 h ABAQUS; 34 h FEBio.
- **Conclusions and limitations:** The method produced similar acceptable future OA classifications across solvers despite different absolute stresses and volumes. Limitations included modeling only the medial compartment, assumed load sharing and generic gait, no subject-specific material properties or local cartilage/bone morphology, low OA-knee numbers, and comparison of only two solvers.
- **Tongue-pressure findings:** None reported; this is a knee-modeling study.
- **Text visibility:** Detailed full-text content is visible, not only the abstract.

- **Authors:** А.О. Мельник (Альона Олександрівна Мельник); І.А. Лазарєв (Ігор Альбертович Лазарєв); О.А. Канюра (Олександр Андрійович Канюра); А.В. Копчак (Андрій Володимирович Копчак); В.В. Філоненко (Валерій Володимирович Філоненко).
- **Year:** 2026; published 2026-03-31.
- **Journal:** *Харківський стоматологічний журнал*, 3(1(7)), 53–63.
- **DOI:** 10.26565/3083-5607-2026-7-04.
- **Species:** Not stated.
- **Sample size (n):** Not stated.
- **Loading/pressures:** Tongue-pressure loading was applied at the alveolar processes and teeth of the upper and lower jaws. Pressure magnitude is not reported in the visible content; no kPa or g/cm² values are given.
- **Measurements:** Maximum nodal displacement (**Total Deformation**); stress distribution (**Equivalent stress**); strain distribution (**Equivalent elastic strain**). Numerical results for these measures are not provided.

- **FE solver(s), boundary conditions, solver-comparison metrics/results:** Not stated.
- **Main conclusions:** The tongue-pressure-induced nodal displacement pattern was said to correspond to the normal facial growth vector in childhood and adolescence. Stress-concentration regions identified as important for mandibular growth and development were the symphysis, body, external oblique line, and base and neck of the condylar process. Maxillary stress concentrations were reported at the anterior maxilla along the inferior and lateral margins of the piriform aperture, the base of the nasal septum, pterygomaxillary sutures, zygomatic arch base, nasal bridge, zygomaticofrontal junction, alveolar process, and anterior teeth. Loads were reported to redistribute across the facial skull and, to a lesser extent, the cranial vault.

MucosaReview.content:
**Article:** “Biomechanics of oral mucosa”  
**Authors:** Junning Chen, Rohana Ahmad, Wei Li, Michael Swain, and Qing Li  
**Year:** 2015

**Exact statement about the pressure thresholds:**

> “The mucosa exhibits a higher tolerance to intermittent than continuous pressure, as the threshold for the alveolar ridge resorption was 19.6 kPa for the former and 6.86 kPa for the latter [10]. A high level of continuous pressure can induce more severe ridge resorption [11]. At the other extreme, continuous pressure less than 1.96 kPa (9.8 kPa for intermittent) caused no bone resorption [10], though apposition was also inhibited [11].”

| Finding | Pressure and loading condition | Reference |
|---|---:|---|
| Threshold for alveolar ridge resorption | 19.6 kPa, intermittent pressure | [10] |
| Threshold for alveolar ridge resorption | 6.86 kPa, continuous pressure | [10] |
| No bone resorption | Continuous pressure less than 1.96 kPa | [10] |
| No bone resorption | Intermittent pressure less than 9.8 kPa | [10] |
| Apposition also inhibited | At the low-pressure conditions described in the quoted statement | [11] |

**References cited for these findings:**

- **[10]** Sato T, Hara T, Mori S, Shirai H, Minagi S. 1998. “Threshold for bone resorption induced by continuous and intermittent pressure in the rat hard palate.”
- **[11]** Imai Y, Sato T, Mori S, Okamoto M. 2002. “A histomorphometric analysis on bone dynamics in denture supporting tissue under continuous pressure.”

| Comparison and results | Qualitatively similar overall responses for individual teeth under incisive versus right-molar bite force. Strain was maximal in the soft-tissue follicle compared with surrounding bone. No quantitative cross-solver comparison or agreement metrics are reported. |
| Conclusions and limitations | Authors propose that follicular soft tissues detect bite-force-induced bone strain and direct remodelling at the inner surface of the surrounding bony crypt, enabling eruption. The abstract does not state limitations. |

Ledogar2016.content:
- **Cadaver and trials:** In vitro validation used a CT-scanned **male human cadaver, aged 42**. The article says two human heads were used for cortical-bone property measurements; the male specimen was scanned and tested before bone samples were removed. **Three in vitro loading trials** were performed for left **P³** biting.
- **Load:** The test simulated a left P³ bite; the supplementary-material description identifies an **INSTRON** loading machine. **Load magnitude and the detailed method of applying the in vitro load are not stated** in the provided page content.
- **Gauges/sites:** Strain was measured at **14 craniofacial locations** and compared with corresponding FEM sites.
- **FE software and properties:** Models were analyzed in **Strand7**. Reported human cortical-bone Young’s modulus values ranged **17.92–25.52 GPa** (mean **20.61 GPa**, SD **1.92**); Poisson’s ratio was **0.293**. The page does not separately specify the validation model’s site-by-site properties.
- **Boundary conditions:** The validation FEM replicated the in vitro loading, but its specific validation boundary conditions are not detailed. For the study’s general bite simulations, the working-side TMJ node was constrained against translation in all axes; the balancing-side TMJ was constrained superoinferiorly and anteroposteriorly; the center of the P³ occlusal surface was constrained superoinferiorly.
- **Regression (log-transformed strain):** Maximum principal strain: **0.845x + 0.194**, **R² = 0.909**, *p* < 0.001. Minimum principal strain: **0.849x + 0.186**, **R² = 0.953**, *p* < 0.001.
- **Percent error (maximum/minimum principal strain, sites 1–14):** 1: **6.67%/45.16%**; 2: **23.08%/14.29%**; 3: **80.00%/40.00%**; 4: **5.43%/5.56%**; 5: **26.67%/18.18%**; 6: **5.71%/36.36%**; 7: **0.79%/27.14%**; 8: **12.60%/4.26%**; 9: **4.35%/50.00%**; 10: **49.26%/10.45%**; 11: **7.04%/21.88%**; 12: **6.48%/15.50%**; 13: **0.86%/22.73%**; 14: **37.35%/40.94%**.
- **Error sources:** Percentage errors could be large at low-strain sites (site 3’s 80% maximum-principal-strain error equaled only **2.67 μɛ**). Other likely contributors noted were modeling the thin anterior maxillary-sinus wall and simplifications of thin nasal-cavity bones.
- **Craniomodel count:** **Seven** human crania were modeled for the main analysis; the specimen-specific validation FEM was an **eighth** model.
